\chapter{Two spoken requests, gently joined}
\label{ch:sa-person-and-quiet-requests}
\hlchaptermodality{271}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can retrieve one person request and one quiet request from meaning.}

Complete chapter 271 by independently retrieving both spoken requests a second time.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{अध्यापकः} \sk{कुत्र} \sk{अस्ति}? (adhyāpakaḥ kutra …)}{अध्यापकः कुत्र अस्ति? (adhyāpakaḥ kutra …)}]{Ask for a familiar person}

\label{lesson:SA-C271-ask-for-a-person}



\begin{quote}
Recall three known pieces: \textbf{\sk{अध्यापकः}}, “teacher”; \textbf{\sk{कुत्र}}, “where?”; and \textbf{\sk{अस्ति}}, “is.”
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: build the person request}]
Put the familiar person first, then the familiar location question:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\sk{अध्यापकः} \sk{कुत्र} \sk{अस्ति}?}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{adhyāpakaḥ kutra asti?}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
“Where is the teacher?”
\end{quote}

Nothing in this turn is a new noun or question word. The new skill is the complete turn: asking where a familiar person is so you can speak with them.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
You arrive at school and need the teacher. Ask where the teacher is.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\textbf{\sk{अध्यापकः} \sk{कुत्र} \sk{अस्ति}?} (\emph{adhyāpakaḥ kutra asti?}) is one bounded way to ask for a familiar person. It does not establish a general service-counter script.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask: “Where is the teacher?”
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{कृपया} \sk{तूष्णीं} \sk{भव} (kṛpayā tūṣṇīṃ bhava)}{कृपया तूष्णीं भव (kṛpayā tūṣṇīṃ bhava)}]{\sk{कृपया} \sk{तूष्णीं} \sk{भव} — please be quiet}

\label{lesson:SA-C271-request-quiet}



\begin{quote}
Recall \textbf{\sk{कृपया}}, “please,” and the complete person request from the previous lesson.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{कृपया} \sk{तूष्णीं} \sk{भव}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\sk{कृपया} \sk{तूष्णीं} \sk{भव।}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{kṛpayā tūṣṇīṃ bhava.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
“Please be quiet.”
\end{quote}

The Board of School Education Haryana copy of the NCERT Class 10 \href{https://bseh.org.in/uploads/ebooks/20\_Class\_10th\_Shemushi\_Sansktit\_120pp.pdf}{\emph{Śemuṣī} Sanskrit reader} uses the exact command \textbf{\sk{तूष्णीं} \sk{भव}}. The grammatical commentary on \href{https://sanskritdocuments.org/learning\_tools/ashtadhyayi/vyakhya/3/3.4.63.htm}{Pāṇini 3.4.63} also explicitly treats \textbf{\sk{तूष्णीम्}} with √\sk{भू}. The \textbf{\sk{कृपया}} at the front is the “please” you already know.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one complete request}]
This lesson owns the complete familiar-person request. It does not teach the imperative paradigm, and it does not license you to manufacture other command forms from \textbf{\sk{भव}}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
A familiar person is speaking while you need silence. Ask politely: “Please be quiet.”

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the complete sourced request for “Please be quiet”?
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(independent spoken-request retrieval …]{Two spoken requests: round one}

\label{lesson:SA-C271-spoken-requests-first-retrieval}



\begin{quote}
Prepare to retrieve two complete spoken turns from meaning.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn: independent retrieval}
No Sanskrit model is shown before you answer.

Say the Sanskrit for these two turns, in order: “Where is the teacher?” Then: “Please be quiet.”

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built: check after answering}]
Now check: \textbf{\sk{अध्यापकः} \sk{कुत्र} \sk{अस्ति}?} (\emph{adhyāpakaḥ kutra asti?}) asks where the teacher is. \textbf{\sk{कृपया} \sk{तूष्णीं} \sk{भव।}} (\emph{kṛpayā tūṣṇīṃ bhava.}) asks a familiar person, politely, to be quiet.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
You have retrieved two bounded turns once without a visible model. That is not a claim of general command formation or conversation-wide ability.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(independent spoken-request retrieval …]{Two spoken requests: round two}

\label{lesson:SA-C271-spoken-requests-final-retrieval}



\begin{quote}
Prepare to retrieve the same two turns in a fresh order.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn: independent retrieval in a fresh order}
No Sanskrit model is shown before you answer.

Say the Sanskrit for these two turns in reverse order: “Please be quiet.” Then: “Where is the teacher?”

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built: check after answering}]
Now check: \textbf{\sk{कृपया} \sk{तूष्णीं} \sk{भव।}} (\emph{kṛpayā tūṣṇīṃ bhava.}) is the quiet request. \textbf{\sk{अध्यापकः} \sk{कुत्र} \sk{अस्ति}?} (\emph{adhyāpakaḥ kutra asti?}) is the person request.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
You can retrieve these two bounded spoken acts twice without a visible model. This is not evidence of general imperative mastery, conversational competence, human validation, learner attainment, or exam readiness.
\end{tcolorbox}
